t: Distribute Repeating Integers: Bitmask Assignment of Customers to Value Buckets
o: Each customer must receive exactly quantity[i] copies of one single value, and values cannot be split between customers, so the identity of the numbers in nums is irrelevant — only the multiset of counts per distinct value matters. With at most 50 unique values but up to 100000 elements, compressing nums into frequency counts is the key preprocessing step. The tiny customer count (m <= 10) signals subset enumeration: 1024 customer masks are cheap to track, so we decide which subset of unsatisfied customers each value bucket feeds; leftovers are simply wasted. Example 2 succeeds because value 3 occurs twice and covers the lone order of 2 while 1 and 2 go unused; example 1 fails because no value occurs twice.
k: Compress nums into frequency counts first — at most 50 buckets drive the whole search regardless of n = 100000.
A value can satisfy any customer subset whose total demand fits its count, since unused leftovers cost nothing.
m <= 10 invites bitmask DP: a 10-bit mask records which customers are already satisfied, and submask enumeration costs O(3^m) total.

a.n: Approach 1: Memoized Backtracking over Values and Customer Subsets
a.i: Process distinct values one at a time; for each, either skip it or hand it a nonempty subset of not-yet-served customers whose demand fits. Recursion asks whether remaining values can finish the rest, and caching on (valueIndex, servedMask) keeps repeated states cheap. Sorting quantity descending commits the tightest orders first, pruning hopeless branches early.
s: Count frequencies of nums into a list of counts (size <= 50); sort quantity descending.
Precompute subsetSum[mask] for all 2^m masks via the lowest set bit.
dfs(i, mask) returns whether the complement of mask can be served using counts[i..].
Enumerate every submask sub of the unsatisfied complement; if subsetSum[sub] <= counts[i], recurse dfs(i+1, mask|sub).
Answer dfs(0, 0), memoized in a hash map keyed by (i, mask).
a.t: O(k * 3^m) worst case — k <= 50 value indices, each expanding every submask of the free set across all masks; pruning usually far less.
a.sp: O(k * 2^m) — the memo table plus the subset-demand array.

a.i: Same recurrence computed iteratively: dp[served] means exactly the customers in that mask are satisfiable with the values processed so far. Each new value copies the previous layer (value unused) and adds transitions from every feasible mask to mask|sub when the subset demand fits the count. No recursion stack, predictable memory, and trivially extensible with bitset tricks.
s: Build need[mask] for all 2^m masks as before.
Initialize dp[0] = true for the empty served set.
For each count c: next = copy(dp); for each feasible mask enumerate submasks sub of the complement and set next[mask|sub] |= need[sub] <= c.
a.t: O(k * 3^m + n) — building subset demands is O(2^m); each of k <= 50 values sweeps masks and their submasks (summing to 3^m per layer).
a.sp: O(2^m) — two boolean layers over customer subsets.

w: Say the bitmask idea out loud early — m <= 10 and 'at most 50 unique values' are the giveaway that the intended solution is exponential in customers and linear in values. Pitfalls: comparing against distinct value identities instead of counts; forgetting the empty-submask case (a value may serve nobody) in the bottom-up version; skipping the descending sort on quantity, which wrecks backtracking pruning. Edge cases: a single order larger than every count returns false; duplicate quantities are fine because masks distinguish customers, not demands. Follow-ups: report the actual assignment by storing parent pointers, or scale m up where meet-in-the-middle or flow-based formulations become necessary.
